narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your undergraduate GPA, your LSAT score, and your grades in the third year of law school. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.20 was the strongest reason for the rejection. It is well below the average of 3.23 among students who were accepted, and this low performance strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to struggle with the bar exam. Your LSAT score of 31 was the second most important factor; it sits noticeably below the 37.18 average of accepted students and also pulled the prediction toward failure. Your third-year law school grades, which placed you in the 5th decile compared with an average around the 5.8th decile for accepted students, worked in the opposite direction and modestly supported a chance of passing, but this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the first two factors.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and consider strengthening any additional academic record you can build before reapplying.
